content:
Each \(T\)-shaped polyomino covers \(4\) unit squares, so a \(6\times6\) grid can contain at most
\[
\left\lfloor \frac{36}{4}\right\rfloor=9
\]
of them.

Now color the \(6\times6\) grid like a chessboard, with \(18\) black and \(18\) white squares. Every \(T\)-polyomino covers either \(3\) black and \(1\) white square or \(1\) black and \(3\) white squares. If \(9\) such pieces filled the board completely, let \(x\) be the number covering \(3\) black squares and \(y\) the number covering \(1\) black square. Then
\[
x+y=9,\qquad 3x+y=18,\qquad x+3y=18.
\]
The last two equations imply \(x=y\), so \(x+y=2x\) must be even, contradicting \(x+y=9\). Hence \(9\) pieces are impossible.

It remains to show \(8\) are possible. The following diagram shows a valid placement, where each letter denotes one \(T\)-piece and each dot is empty:
\[
\begin{array}{cccccc}
A&A&A&B&E&.\\
D&A&B&B&E&E\\
D&D&C&B&E&.\\
D&C&C&C&.&F\\
G&G&G&H&F&F\\
.&G&H&H&H&F
\end{array}
\]
Thus the maximum number is
\[
\boxed{8}.
\]
